mcItems.q: What is the primary definition of an interval in music theory?
op: A) The ratio between two sonic frequencies.
B) The difference in pitch between two sounds.
C) The ratio between two sonic frequencies and two sounds.
D) The difference in pitch between two sounds and scale steps.
mcItems.ex: Option B is correct because an interval is defined as the difference in pitch between two sounds (claims[0]). Option A is a physical description, not the primary theoretical definition. Option C combines two distinct concepts. Option D incorrectly conflates intervals with scale steps.

mcItems.q: When comparing the relationship between two notes in a scale, what term describes the interval between successive notes?
mcItems.ex: Option B is correct because intervals between successive notes of a scale are also known as scale steps (claims[2]). Option D is too broad, as an interval can exist between any two notes, not just successive ones. Option A and C relate to chordal/harmonic structure, not sequential scale relations.

mcItems.q: What is the fundamental structure of a triad?
op: A set of four notes forming a fourth above the root
B a set of three notes stacked vertically in thirds
C a chord consisting of a triad plus a seventh above the root
D a chord with four notes in a descending pattern
mcItems.ex: B is correct because a triad is a set of three notes stacked vertically in thirds. A common error is confusing this with a seventh chord, which adds an extra note.

mcItems.q: How does the addition of a seventh chord affect the triad?
op: A it stabilizes the triad and emphasizes static movement
B it destabilizes the triad and allows emphasis in a given direction
C it maintains the triad's structure without change
D it only affects the intervallic relationships within the triad
mcItems.ex: B is correct because the seventh destabilizes the triad, allowing emphasis in a given direction. Misconception is that the seventh chord always stabilizes the underlying triad.

mcItems.q: What is the fundamental structure of a triad?
op: A set of four notes forming a fourth above the root
B a set of three notes stacked vertically in thirds
C a chord consisting of a triad plus a seventh above the root
D a chord with four notes in a descending pattern
mcItems.ex: B is correct because a triad is a set of three notes stacked vertically in thirds. A common error is confusing this with a seventh chord, which adds an extra note.

keyTerms.df: A set of three notes (or "pitch classes") that can be stacked vertically in thirds.
keyTerms.eg: C-E-G in C major.
keyTerms.mi: Confusing a triad with a seventh chord.
keyTerms.cx: A triad is defined by three notes stacked in thirds, whereas a seventh chord includes an additional note.

keyTerms.df: A chord consisting of a triad plus a note forming an interval of a seventh above the chord's root.
keyTerms.eg: C-E-G-B in C major.
keyTerms.mi: Believing a seventh chord is just a triad with an added note.
keyTerms.cx: A seventh chord is specifically a triad augmented by a seventh above the root, not just any extra note.

mcItems.q: What is the primary definition of an interval in music theory?
op: A) The ratio between two sonic frequencies.
B) The difference in pitch between two sounds.
C) The ratio between two sonic frequencies and two sounds.
D) The difference in pitch between two sounds and scale steps.
mcItems.ex: Option B is correct because an interval is defined as the difference in pitch between two sounds (claims[0]). Option A is a physical description, not the primary theoretical definition. Option C combines two distinct concepts. Option D incorrectly conflates intervals with scale steps.
